An obesity paradox is a term that, in certain populations, 
people who are obese seem to live longer. This paradox 
has also been observed in sepsis populations, although its 
validity remains controversial[2].

al. analyzed the MIMIC-IV dataset to investigate mortality in 
sepsis patients and concluded that, unlike older patients, those under the age of 50 
did not exhibit the obesity paradox[3].
•
Elkan
 
Matan
 
et
 
al
. analyzed the sepsis patients admitted to Shamir Medical Center, 
Israel, and concluded higher body mass index(BMI) is a protective factor against 
mortality in both elderly(over 80 years of age) and younger patients[4].
• Obesity was defined as BMI≥30 kg/m² according to Centers for Disease Control and 
Prevention (CDC) criteria.
• Elderly individuals were classified based on the World Health Organization’s criteria 
(≥65 years).
The obesity paradox in sepsis patients was generally evident across age groups and those with 
chronic conditions, but was not observed in elderly patients without chronic disease.
DISCUSSION
• Why was obesity paradox absent only in elderly patients without chronic condition? 
➢ One possible explanation is that obesity may provide metabolic protection against sepsis in patients with chronic diseases—conditions that are persistent or 
long-lasting and can alter inflammatory and metabolic responses[1].
➢ However, in elderly patients without such conditions may not benefit from these protective interactions, as age-related immune dysregulation may override 
these potential advantages of excess adiposity.
